A deep eutectic solvent pretreatment with self-cleaning lignin droplets function to efficiently improve the enzymatic saccharification and ethanol production of bamboo residues
Qinpei Hou c, Zhaoming Liu c, Zhengjun Shi a,b, Haiyan Yang a,b,c, Dawei Wang b,c, Jing Yang a,b,c, *

ª Key Laboratory for Forest Resources Conservation and Utilization in the Southwest Mountains of China, Ministry of Education, Southwest Forestry University, Kunming 650224, China ᵇ Key Laboratory for Yunnan Province Universities on Chemical Utilization of Forestry Lignocellulosic Biomass, Education of Department of Yunnan Province, Kunming 650224, China ᶜ School of Materials and Chemical Engineering, Southwest Forestry University, Kunming 650224, China
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Bamboo residues Deep eutectic solvent pretreatment Lignin droplets Enzymatic hydrolysis Ethanol production

ABSTRACT Bamboo is considered a promising biomass resource for solving the energy crisis and climate change. Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC) as a hydrogen bond acceptor, was used to synthesize a new deep eutectic solvent (DES) with self-cleaning lignin droplets function during the bamboo pretreatment. When D. giganteus were pretreated with DES of DMC and oxalic acid (OA) at 130 °C for 4 h, about 96% of xylan and 81% of lignin were removed from the bamboo wastes, and 54.44% of glucose yield and 13.5 g/L of ethanol production were achieved. Compared with the native lignin from raw bamboo, the molecular weight and β-O-4 aryl ethers in the regenerated lignin fractions were significantly decreased. In addition, the DMC/OA pretreatment reduced the lignin droplets and surface lignin content of pretreated substrates by comparison with choline chloride (ChCl)based DES pretreatment, leading to more cellulose substrates exposed. The enzymatic digestibility of DMC/OA-treated bamboo was 4 times higher than that of ChCl/OA. This work provided insights to the discovery of more functional DESs for the biorefinery of lignocellulosic biomass.

1. Introduction Bamboo, due to its fast growth rate (3–5 years) and chemical composition similar to wood, has become a promising biomass resource in biorefinery system (Scurlock, et al., 2000). Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro are planted widely in the southwest of China, and it was used as feedstock in the food, textile, construction, and papermaking industry. During these processes, approximately 3 million tons or more of bamboo processing residue are left annually (Liang et al., 2023). These bamboo wastes can be processed into sugar-based compounds and bioethanol through chemical or biochemical methods, which can reduce waste management and environmental pollution issues, and also provide sustainability for energy resources.
Pretreatment technology was required to destroy the native recal- citrant structure of bamboo, making it easier for the carbohydrate

fraction to hydrolyze into monosaccharides, and then ferment into ethanol (Ahmed et al., 2022; Anu et al., 2020). Deep eutectic solvent (DES) prepared with hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA) at proper ratios has attracted much interests of researcher due to ease of synthesis, less toxic, biodegradable, and low cost (Ahmed et al., 2022; Lugani et al., 2020). The biomass pretreatment of DES can efficiently remove non-crystalline complexes, such as hemicellulose and lignin, by breaking the lignin-carbohydrate linkages and ether bonds of lignin matrix (Jose et al., 2023; Areeya et al., 2023). Choline chloride (ChCl) was widely adopted as HBA in the synthesis of DES for biomass pre- treatment. A detailed discussion on ChCl-based DES pretreatment of lignocellulose have been proposed. Many studies have shown that the ChCl-based DES was a good solvent for lignin solubility and choline chloride increased the β-O-4 cleavage rate of milled wood lignin (Smink et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020). The chloride ions can

help cleave lignin carbohydrate complexes (LCCs) of biomass, and the formation of new strong hydrogen bonds between Cl - in DES and hy- droxyl groups in carbohydrates and lignin, can weaken the hydrogen bond network inside lignocellulose, which can result in the dissolution of biomass components (Liu et al., 2017; Wang et al., 2020). In addition, Li's group have reported that the hydroxyl groups of lignin could un- dergo nucleophilic substitution by chloride anions, resulting in the for- mation of stable intermediates that facilitate the cleavage of lignin ether bonds (Li et al., 2018).

Although the ChCl-based DES system has shown excellent perfor-mance in lignocellulose fractionation, other HBAs with special functions have also attracted the attention of some researchers, which had high biomass pretreatment performance and special functions in cracking the LCC linkages of biomass (Selkälä et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2023). Recently, Tang et al. (2023) reported a new type of DES with additional functions using CTAB and LA. They found that CTAB not only prevented the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin, but sol-ubilized some waxes on the substrates, significantly improving the accessibility of pretreated rice husks. Our previous results showed that DES pretreatment of tetramethylammonium chloride and oxalic acid can produce some lignin droplets on the pretreated substrates, which reduced the degradability of bamboo. These lignin droplets that affect carbohydrate bioconversion can be removed through washing the pre-treated residues with dilute alkaline solution (Yang et al., 2022). Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC), as an active monomer with unsaturated ethylene and quaternary ammonium salt groups, is widely used in the synthesis of various functional polymers, for example, polymerization of methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (PDMC). The synthesis process of DMC has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation (Deng et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016). Therefore, DMC, as a quaternary ammonium salt with longer alkyl chains, can also serve as a HBA in DES synthesis to form hydrogen bonds with hydrogen bond donors (HBD).

The main objective of this study was to develop an innovative DMC-based DES pretreatment with self-cleaning functions, which can prevent the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin and lignin droplets during the bamboo pretreatment. The process parameters of DMC/OA pretreatment were optimized and discussed in terms of the removal of lignin and xylan, as well as enzymatic digestibility and bioethanol production. And complete characterizations (BET surface area, XRD, SEM, XPS, hydrophobicity, and FTIR technology) were further performed on the substrates to explain the mechanism of DMC-based DES pretreatment. And the native lignin in bamboo and regenerated DES lignin fraction were collected; the GPC and 2D-HSQC NMR techniques were used to characterize their chemical structure. Finally, the hydrogen bond number and interaction energy were measured to further explore the interaction mechanism between DMC-based DES system and bamboo biomass.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials *Dendrocalamus giganteus* Munro (*D. giganteus*, DG) harvested from Yunnan Province, China, was milled into bamboo powder (40–60 mesh) and dried in an oven at 40 °C for 10 h. Cellulase enzyme (CellicCTec2 with 220 FPU/mL and Celluclast 1.5 L with protein content of 40 mg/mL) was supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai). *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* from Yichang Angel Yeast Company was used during the ethanol fermentation.

2.2. DES pretreatment of bamboo residues The DMC (HBA) and oxalic acid (HBD) of different molar ratio were mixed at 90 °C until a homogeneous liquid formed. The Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters (α, β, and π*) were adopted to characterize these

DES systems (Xue et al., 2016). Bamboo powder was pretreated with DMC-based DES at 110–140 °C and various times (3–8 h) with stirring of 150 rpm. The solid/liquid ratio of DG and DES was 1:10 (g/mL). After the pretreatment, the mixture was filtered using Brinell funnel, and the solid fractions were washed until neutral. The bamboo pretreated with DES was dried overnight in the oven of 40 °C for enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation. The liquid fraction was acidified to pH 2 with sulfuric acid to precipitate lignin. The lignin obtained was referred to as DMC/OA lignin. And the supernatant was collected for the DES recovery. The DES pretreated samples under the different conditions were named as DMC/OA-110 for the pretreatment temperature of 110 °C, DMC/OA-3 for pretreatment temperature of 3 h, and DMC/OA-1:1 for the DMC/OA ratio of 1:1, respectively.

At the same time, bamboo powder pretreated with DES of ChCl/OA or liquid water hot under (LWH) a ratio of 1:10 (w/v) and 130 °C for 4 h was taken as control. The treated bamboo powder was labeled as ChCl/ OA-DG and LHW-DG, respectively. The NREL standard method was used to analyze the chemical composition of untreated and pretreated bamboo (Sluiter et al., 2011). The removal of xylan, delignification and glucan recovery after pretreatment were obtained by the formulas given below:

Xylan removal (%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{xylan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{xylan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (1) Delignification(%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{lignin in treated bamboo(g)}}{\text{lignin in the raw biomass(g)}}$ × 100 (2) Glucan recovery(%) = $\frac{\text{glucan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{glucan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (3)

2.3. Enzymatic saccharification and fermentation of bamboo wastes Enzymatic hydrolysis of samples was operated in an air incubator (150 rpm and 50 °C) at 2 wt% solid concentration and 50 mM sodium citrate buffer solution for 72 h. The cellulase (Cellic® CTec2) was loaded at 20 FPU/g biomass. The hydrolysate was centrifuged and then analyzed the content of reducing sugars using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). On the other hand, Tween 80 of 150 mg/g substrates was added to further enhance the yield of glucose and xylose during the enzymatic hydrolysis.

The enzymatic hydrolysate (16 mL) and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (3 g/L) were mixed at 35 °C for 24 h. The content of sugars and ethanol in the fermented broth were analyzed by HPLC (Agilent Technologies, 1260 series, USA), equipped with a Bio-Rad HPX-87 H column. The enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency and bioethanol production were calcu- lated, in accordance with our previous publications (Meng et al., 2023).

2.4. Cellulase adsorption study of treated biomass Enzymatic adsorption capacity was determined at 4 °C and 150 rpm by combining 10 mg of bamboo powder with the concentration range of (0.01–2) mg/mL cellulase solution (Yang et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023). The adsorption isotherms with different enzymatic concentrations were studied by UV-vis spectrophotometry after 3 h adsorption balance. The enzymatic adsorption capacity on solid residue were obtained by Langmuir isothermal adsorption equation (Γ = Гmax KC/(1+KC)), Γ and Γmax (mg/g) are the equilibrium and maximum adsorption capacity, respectively. C (mg/mg) the concentration of enzyme protein in the liquid. K (mL/mg cellulase) the constant of Langmuir. And the R (R=Γ max ×K) is the distribution coefficient (L/g). All pretreatment, enzyme hydrolysis and adsorption experiments were performed in triplicate.

2.5. Structural characterization analysis of pretreated bamboo residues

The hydrophobicity and accessibility of DG were determined using Rose Bengal dye and Congo red dye (DR 28) adsorption method (Gessner et al., 2000; Inglesby and Zeronian, 2002). The average DPs were evaluated using copper ethylene-diamine solvent method (Lin et al., 2021). Using the Ultima IV XRD instrument (Rigaku Corporation, Japan) to analyze crystallinity index (CrI) of the substrates, and the CrI/cellu-lose content was used to evaluate the actual effect of DES pretreatment on CrI (Pihlajaniemi et al., 2016). FTIR was determined using the KBr press method with a sample to KBr mass ratio of 1:10 and analyzed by 710 FTIR spectrophotometer (Nicolet, USA) over 4000–400 cm⁻¹. Dry samples were sprayed with gold powder for 30–90 s, and then adhered to conductive adhesive for SEM analysis (Sigma 300, Germany, 10 kv). The relative surface area was measured by Micromeritics ASAP2460 analyzer instrument (USA). XPS spectra were obtained on an Escalab 250Xi spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific Inc., US), and the surface coverage by lignin (Slig) and carbohydrates (Scarb) were estimated using the research of Meng et al. (2023). The weight of number-average mo-lecular (Mn) and weight-average molecular (Mw) for willed wood lignin (MWL)and DES-lignin samples were obtained using Gel Permeation Chromatography (GPC) analysis (Waters E2695, America). Additionally, a Bruker AVIII 600 MHz M instrument was used to conduct the nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) spectra of the lignin samples.

The optimization of molecular structures was achieved using the ORCA program, which employed the density functional B3LYP D3 method and the def2-TZVP basis set (Frank, 2022). In addition, the electrostatic potential distribution (ESP) of DES was analyzed using the Multiwfn program, and the VMD program was utilized for visualization

purposes (Lu and Chen, 2012, Humphrey et al., 1996). Classic molecular dynamics simulations were carried out to investigate the mixed solution from the atomic level. Cellobiose, 4-O-methyl Gluconic acid xylose and Veratrylglycerol-β-guaiacyl ether (VG) was selected as the cellulose, hemicellulose and lignin model, respectively. Kinetic simulations of cellulose-hemicellulose-lignin without DES were first conducted as a control group, and then the two DES systems were added. The number of hydrogen bonding, interaction energy and free volume of these system during the kinetic simulations were analyzed using GROMACS 2020 program.

## 3. Results and discussion ### 3.1. Evaluation of DMC/OA pretreatment efficiency The pretreatment performance was evaluated according to xylan and lignin removal, and release of fermentable sugars in Fig. 1. The raw DG contained 47.42% of glucan, 16.61% of xylan, 28.31% of lignin, which was carried out the DMC/OA pretreatment under different conditions. It was found that the solid residue recovery by the DMC/OA pretreatment decreased to about 60% in Fig. 1a-c, indicating that part of the raw bamboo has been dissolved. As seen in Figure1a, the molar ratio of DMC and OA especially affected the DES pretreatment performance. As the molar ratio of DMC and OA increased from 1:1 to 3:1, the removal of xylan was 96.88%, 96.99% and 94.52% respectively, without significant changes. It is noteworthy that an obvious increase in delignification (79.56%, 81.53% and 87.52%) were observed, suggesting that the dosage of DMC played a critical role in improving the solubility and degradability of lignin. As the concentration of DMC increased, the delignification also increased, but the enzymatic hydrolysis yield showed a trend of first increasing and then decreasing, implying that there are some factors that affect the enzymatic saccharification efficiency especially under high temperature conditions, apart from the content of lignin and xylan. Besides, when the molar ratio of DMC and OA decreased to 1:2, the removal of xylan and lignin, and glucan recovery were 98.79%, 18.56% and 81.20% respectively. The subsequent enzyme hydrolysis yield was only 10.3%. This was mainly due to the fact that the high lignin content was the main factor decreasing enzyme saccharification. This suggested that more H+ cannot damage the DG structure in DMC-based DES system, due to the proton attacking bamboo within the system had been saturated. As a result, the 2:1 molar ratio of DMC and OA was selected for DMC-based DES pretreatment.

The temperature during the DMC/OA pretreatment also greatly impacted chemical compositions in Fig. 1b. After increasing the pretreatment temperature from 110 to 140 °C, the xylan removal reached about 98%, and the delignification was increased from 59.61% to 85.34%. Meanwhile, the glucan retention slowly increased from 79.47% to 88.24%, suggesting that most of the glucan was retained in the substrate. The optimal reaction temperature was 130 °C, providing an enzymatic saccharification efficiency of 54.44%. Fig. 1c showed the effect of pretreatment time on chemical composition of bamboo. The xylan removal slightly improved, and the delignification was 86.40%, 81.53%, 68.96% and 61.95% respectively, when the time was extended from 3 to 8 h. And longer pretreatment time also can cause more glucan loss. It was noted that 4 h provided the highest enzymatic digestibility (54.44%), which was followed by 3 h (50.12%), 6 h (47.01%) and 8 h (36.12%). Therefore, 4 h was used as the appropriative pretreatment time in this study.

All the pretreatments including liquid hot water (LHW), ChCL/OA and DMC/OA DES system were conducted at 130°C for 4 h. In a controlled reaction of LHW without DES (Fig. 1d), a few amounts of lignin and xylan (19.54% and 14.53%) were removed. When bamboo powder was pretreated with DES of ChCL/OA at 130°C for 4 h, the solid residue recovery was 63.12%, almost all xylans have been removed, and its delignification slightly increased to 23.16%. This result suggested that the ChCL/OA and DMC/OA pretreatments led to similar removal of xylan from bamboo. This may be because the dissociated protons of organic acids in DES system may break the hydrogen bond and inter- molecular force between glucan and xylan, leading to the xylan removal (Ji et al., 2021). However, DMC/OA pretreatment under the optimal pretreatment conditions showed higher delignification (81.545) compared with ChCL/OA-DG (23.16%). Correspondingly, an increase of 4-7 times in saccharification efficiency of DMC/OA-DG was obtained. Because ChCL-based and DMC-based DES are both acidic DES systems,

they can remove most of bamboo hemicellulose under high temperature conditions. However, there are certain differences in their delignifica- tion ability and substrate characteristics. Loow et al. (2017) and Kohli et al. (2020) had reported that Kamlet-Taft parameters in DES system and formation of hydrogen bonds between DES were critical factors affecting the dissolution of lignin and xylan.

3.2. Enhancing effect of surfactant on enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol production The nonionic surfactant Tween80 is used to improve the enzymatic digestibility and ethanol production of DES-treated samples. The effect of Tween80 on the release of fermentable sugars in the enzymatic saccharification of different treated samples is summarized in Fig. 2a. The addition of Tween80 (150 mg/g substrates) showed a considerable positive effect on enzymatic hydrolysis of raw DG, LHW-DG and ChCL/ OA-DG. The glucose yields were 13.86% and 16.67% and 48.76%, respectively, increased by 2-3.6 folds under the Tween80-assistance. It had reported that addition of Tween 80 during the enzymatic saccharification process can reduce the non-productive cellulase binding to residual lignin and lignin-like materials on the substrates, leaving more cellulase free in liquid to hydrolyze cellulose fraction (Wang et al., 2018; Zhang et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2020). The formation of pseudo-lignin during the ChCL/OA pretreatment of bamboo biomass could as a potential reason for inhibiting enzyme hydrolysis efficiency. Unexpectedly, the addition of Tween80 did not significantly increase the enzymatic digestibility of DMC/OA-DG, and the yield of glucose slightly increased from 54.44% to 55.18%. It is reasonable to speculate that DMC played a crucial role in preventing the deposition of pseudo-lignin formed by by-product polymerization. The mechanism may be similar that of surfactants in the enzymatic hydrolysis.

Ethanol production from hydrolysate of different pretreated substrates was conducted in a 50-mL flask through adding necessary nutrients for yeast growth, and the ethanol concentration can reveal the effects of sugars conversion. As shown in Fig. 2b, glucose levels showed a regular decreasing trend within the first 9 h, mainly because the bioconversion is influenced by the degree of enzymatic saccharification. After 12 h of fermentation, the residual glucose concentrations in all liquids fell below 0.5 g/L, suggesting that S. cerevisiae can effectively consumed glucose in hydrolysate and convert them into ethanol. The ethanol content reached 12.3 g/L in DMC/OA-DG, whereas the ChCL/ OA-DG showed a lower ethanol production of 3.41 g/L. This is mainly because the amount of reducing sugars released from DMC/OA-DG was relatively higher. The maximum ethanol concentrations for DMC/OA-T- DG (13.5 g/L) were obtained due to the addition of Tween80 during the enzymatic hydrolysis, corresponding to the ethanol yields of 79.18%. But there was a small variation in ethanol production compared with DMC/OA-DG. Meanwhile, the ethanol concentration of ChCL/OA-T-DG

3.3. Effect of DMC/OA pretreatment on enzymatic adsorption and cellulose accessibility of bamboo biomass

The effects of different pretreated samples on enzymatic adsorption are shown in Fig. 3. The ability of raw DG in adsorbing cellulase was weak and its maximum amount of adsorbed enzyme (Γmax), Langmuir constant (K) and distribution coefficient (R) were 13.83 mg/g sample, 4.96 mL/mg enzyme and 0.069 g/L, respectively. As shown in the adsorption isotherm, the enzyme adsorption capability on the substrates was promoted with the assistance of LHW and ChCL/OA pretreatment. Their maximum adsorption capacities were 7.08 and 18.03 mg/g sam-ple, increased by about 24% than that of untreated DG. The affinity of cellulase to substrate (the K value) also increased to 15.29 mL/mg for LHW-DG and 17.18 mL/mg for ChCL/OA-DG. Compared with LHW, ChCL/OA pretreatment showed the higher xylan removal yield. Theo-retically, the affinity of its substrate to cellulase should be stronger than LHW, because the xylan removal can result in the increase of substrates porosity. But there was no significant difference in the affinity of cellulase to the two pretreated substrates. This indicated that the surface and structural features of substrates might be the reasons for the inhibited cellulase adsorption on ChCL/OA-DG. However, when DG was performed the DMC/OA pretreatment, it was obvious that the cellulase showed higher affinity to the substrate based on adsorption curve and Langmuir constant (K), resulted in the higher adsorption capacity of cellulase on DMC/OA -DG (Γm=40.68 mg/g), meant that DMC/OA DES pretreatment created more binding sites of DG than the ChCL/OA pre-treatment. Probable reasons for this observation were that the removal of a large amount of lignin and hemicellulose, and the absence of surface covering on the pretreated substrate surface, which will be beneficial for enzyme adsorption and hydrolysis.

The amount of cellulose surface area accessible to cellulase, defined as cellulose accessibility, also were used to predict the pretreatment performance of biomass. In Fig. 4b, the cellulose accessibility of untreated DG was only 55.46 mg dye/(g material), which is lower than that of untreated Moso bamboo (about 120 mg/g) reported by Ling et al. (2021). This was related to the content and structure of cellulose, xylan, and lignin in the raw bamboo. The value increased to 64.52 mg/g and 71.11 after LHW and ChCL/OA pretreatment, respectively. Ling et al. (2021) found that when Moso bamboo were pretreated with ChCL/OA, cellulose accessibility increased to about 135 mg/g, which was similar to the increasing trend of ChCL/OA-DG. Compared with LHW-DG, the ChCL/OA-DG was not more susceptible to enzymatic saccharification

despite having most of xylan removal, and its hydrolysis yield only increased to 13.44%. This observation indicates that some covering may be on the surface of ChCL/OA-DG, causing the decrease of cellulose accessibility and enzyme digestion efficiency. Mao et al. (2010) reported that the limitations of enzymatic hydrolysis for corn stover (CS) were caused by the limited accessibility of cellulose. The DMC/OA pretreat- ment resulted in 3.5-fold delignification than ChCL/OA pretreatment, so the cellulose accessibility of DMC/OA-DG was further improved to 95.15 mg/g, increased by 34% than that of ChCL/OA-DG, which is in accordance with the increase of enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Previ- ous studies have shown a significant positive correlation between the accessibility of cellulose and enzymatic hydrolysis (Sheng et al., 2021). The greater the accessibility of cellulose, the higher the enzymatic hy- drolysis yield of substrates. However, more comprehensive research is needed to understand the impact of DMC/OA pretreatment on cellulose accessibility and enzymatic saccharification of DG bamboo, such as the structural characteristics of substrates and parameters of DMC-based DES solvent system.

3.4. The effects of DMC/OA pretreatment on the physicochemical properties of bamboo residues The characteristics of pretreated substrates are of great significance for exploring the mechanism of DES pretreatment. FTIR spectroscopy was used to study the structural modifications of DG upon DES pretreatment. When DG was used to pretreat with DMC/OA, the peak sizes of C-O and C-O-C groups at 1032 and 1160 cm⁻¹, as well as the stretching vibration of CH₂ at 2930 cm⁻¹ obviously increased in Fig. 4a, indicating an increase in relative cellulose content in the substrate. The disappearance of the two peaks at 1620 and 1511 cm⁻¹ attributed to the lignin aromatic ring indicated lignin removal during the DMC/OA pretreatment process. Furthermore, the peak at around 3340 cm⁻¹ of DMC/OA-DG was broader and deeper, indicating that an enhanced O-H stretching strength of hydrogen bonds in cellulose and lignin.

The hydrophobicity and degree of polymerization (DP) analyses of treated DG are shown in Fig. 4b. The Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters (α, β, and π*) of ChCl/OA and DMC/OA solvents were shown in Fig. 7a. The values of α, β, and π* represented respectively the ability to provide and accept hydrogen bonds, as well as the polarizability of solvents, which can be affected by the structures of DES system. Both ChCl and DMC are quaternary ammonium salts, but the alkyl chain length of DMC is longer than that of ChCl, which can affect the Kamlet-Taft parameters of DES system. As can be seen in Fig. 7a, the increase of α and π* value in ChCl/OA (1.802 and 1.408) was about 6% compared to these of DMC/OA. The α and π* values of two DES systems showed a slight difference due to the similar HBD. Liu et al. (2019) and Yu et al. (2020) reported that the lignin solubility had a positive correlation with the α and π* of DESs, while the xylan solubility had a positive correlation with β. This meant that DES of ChCl/OA should have better lignin solubility than DMC/OA. In addition, it was observed that there was an increasing trend in the β value for ChCl/OA (0.1032) and DMC/OA (0.3678). It indicates that DMC had strong hydrogen bond acceptance ability, thus the DMC/OA solvent system could be a strong ability to break intermolecular hydrogen bonds in biomass, which could lead to the decrease of DP in the cellulose substrate (Fig. 4b). Unfortunately, the hydrogen bonds interactions heightened the viscosity of DMC-based DES. The viscosity DMC/OA (25.41 mPa·s) was higher than the ChCl/OA (15.65 mPa·s). Hernandez
et al. (2013) had reported that viscosity below 90 mPa-s was beneficial for the fluidity and mass transfer of substrates in the pretreatment process.

From the above discussion, multi-effects were revealed in the DMC/ OA pretreatment of bamboo residues. The DES system of DMC/OA with a long the alkyl chain length, had strong hydrogen bond acceptance ability and can destroy the hydrogen bond network structure of bamboo material. And the DMC/OA can not only catalyze the cleavage of the ether or ester bond between lignin and hemicellulose, but disrupted part of cellulose glycosidic bonds, ultimately leading to a decrease in cellu- lose polymerization and crystallinity degree. More importantly, the DMC/OA pretreatment has a significant self-cleaning effect on pseudo- lignin and surface lignin on the substrates. Additionally, due to the dissolution of lignin and xylan in the DMC-based DES system, the changes of hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity properties, crystal structures of cellulose, and cellulose accessibility were beneficial for the enzymatic saccharification. A new type of DMC/OA treated bamboo residue with self-cleaning function has been synthesized, which can clean the lignin droplets formed on the surface of substrate during the pretreatment process, and ultimately improve the enzymatic saccharification efficiency.

### 3.7. Mass balance analysis of ChCl/OA and DMC/OA pretreatment The pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation process of bamboo wastes are described in the mass balance image (Fig. 8). The 1000 g of DG including 474.7 g glucan, 166.1 g xylan and 283.1 g lignin were subjected to the DES pretreatment at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:10 at 130 °C for 4 h. When ChCl/OA was used as pretreatment solvent, 780.3 g of residue was recovered, which consisted of

402.1 g glucan, 1.2 g xylan and 213.7 g lignin. Then 54 g of glucose and a low ethanol content of 3.41 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 61.18%) was obtained during the enzymatic hydrolysis and fermenta- tion of ChCl/OA -DG. However, after DMC/OA pretreatment, 506.1 g pretreated DG were achieved, containing glucan of 411.9 g, xylan of 9.9 g and lignin of 52.4 g, indicating a large amount of lignin and hemicellulose have been removed, while most of the glucan was retained. Glucose of 224.2 g was released from the enzymatic hydrolysis process of DMC/OA-DG, with a glucose yield of 54.44%. The fermen- tation of hydrolysates resulted in the maximum ethanol production of 12.3 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 73.25%), which were 3.6- folds higher compared with that of ChCl/OA -DG.

Previous studies based on various bamboo pretreatment were summarized (see supplementary material). It showed that the DMC-based DES pretreatment performance was at a moderate level among all bamboo pretreatments. The highest enzymatic hydrolysis yield (about 65%) comes from ternary DES pretreatment (ChCl/OA/EG), which is 1.18 times higher than DMC/OA pretreatment. During the pretreatment of ChCl/OA/EG, a third component, ethylene glycol, was required to alleviating the surface lignin and pseudo lignin on the substrates. DES of DMC/OA has similar to the effect of ternary DES pretreatment. Additionally, most methods improved the pretreatment performance of bamboo using the diverse hydrogen donors, while DMC, as hydrogen receptor, has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation, which DMC/OA pretreatment has potential in improving biorefinery efficiency of bamboo and reducing costs.

## 4. Conclusions A new green solvent DMC/OA with the self-cleaning lignin droplets function was used to treat bamboo at 130 °C and a solid-liquid ratio of 2:1 for 4 h. It removed a large amount of lignin and xylan from biomass, and the coverage of surface lignin was reduced to 56%, which increased the enzymatic digestibility by 4 times compared to ChCl-based DES. Higher cellulose accessibility, lower degree of polymerization, hydrophobicity and CrI/cellulose, and more porous structure of DMC/OA-DG were obtained. It provides some useful information for developing the functional DES pretreatment and more green solvents for the bamboo biorefinery.

Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC) as a hydrogen bond acceptor, was used to synthesize a new deep eutectic solvent (DES) with self-cleaning lignin droplets function during the bamboo pretreatment. When D. giganteus were pretreated with DES of DMC and oxalic acid (OA) at 130 °C for 4 h, about 96% of xylan and 81% of lignin were removed from the bamboo wastes, and 54.44% of glucose yield and 13.5 g/L of ethanol production were achieved. Compared with the native lignin from raw bamboo, the molecular weight and β-O-4 aryl ethers in the regenerated lignin fractions were significantly decreased. In addition, the DMC/OA pretreatment reduced the lignin droplets and surface lignin content of pretreated substrates by comparison with choline chloride (ChCl)based DES pretreatment, leading to more cellulose substrates exposed. The enzymatic digestibility of DMC/OA-treated bamboo was 4 times higher than that of ChCl/OA. This work provided insights to the discovery of more functional DESs for the biorefinery of lignocellulosic biomass. 1. Introduction Bamboo, due to its fast growth rate (3–5 years) and chemical composition similar to wood, has become a promising biomass resource in biorefinery system (Scurlock, et al., 2000). Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro are planted widely in the southwest of China, and it was used as feedstock in the food, textile, construction, and papermaking industry. During these processes, approximately 3 million tons or more of bamboo processing residue are left annually (Liang et al., 2023). These bamboo wastes can be processed into sugar-based compounds and bioethanol through chemical or biochemical methods, which can reduce waste management and environmental pollution issues, and also provide sustainability for energy resources. Pretreatment technology was required to destroy the native recal- citrant structure of bamboo, making it easier for the carbohydrate fraction to hydrolyze into monosaccharides, and then ferment into ethanol (Ahmed et al., 2022; Anu et al., 2020). Deep eutectic solvent (DES) prepared with hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA) at proper ratios has attracted much interests of researcher due to ease of synthesis, less toxic, biodegradable, and low cost (Ahmed et al., 2022; Lugani et al., 2020). The biomass pretreatment of DES can efficiently remove non-crystalline complexes, such as hemicellulose and lignin, by breaking the lignin-carbohydrate linkages and ether bonds of lignin matrix (Jose et al., 2023; Areeya et al., 2023). Choline chloride (ChCl) was widely adopted as HBA in the synthesis of DES for biomass pre- treatment. A detailed discussion on ChCl-based DES pretreatment of lignocellulose have been proposed. Many studies have shown that the ChCl-based DES was a good solvent for lignin solubility and choline chloride increased the β-O-4 cleavage rate of milled wood lignin (Smink et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020). In addition, Li's group have reported that the hydroxyl groups of lignin could un- dergo nucleophilic substitution by chloride anions, resulting in the for- mation of stable intermediates that facilitate the cleavage of lignin ether bonds (Li et al., 2018). Although the ChCl-based DES system has shown excellent perfor-mance in lignocellulose fractionation, other HBAs with special functions have also attracted the attention of some researchers, which had high biomass pretreatment performance and special functions in cracking the LCC linkages of biomass (Selkälä et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2023). Recently, Tang et al. (2023) reported a new type of DES with additional functions using CTAB and LA. They found that CTAB not only prevented the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin, but sol-ubilized some waxes on the substrates, significantly improving the accessibility of pretreated rice husks. Our previous results showed that DES pretreatment of tetramethylammonium chloride and oxalic acid can produce some lignin droplets on the pretreated substrates, which reduced the degradability of bamboo. These lignin droplets that affect carbohydrate bioconversion can be removed through washing the pre-treated residues with dilute alkaline solution (Yang et al., 2022). Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC), as an active monomer with unsaturated ethylene and quaternary ammonium salt groups, is widely used in the synthesis of various functional polymers, for example, polymerization of methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (PDMC). The synthesis process of DMC has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation (Deng et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016). Therefore, DMC, as a quaternary ammonium salt with longer alkyl chains, can also serve as a HBA in DES synthesis to form hydrogen bonds with hydrogen bond donors (HBD). The main objective of this study was to develop an innovative DMC-based DES pretreatment with self-cleaning functions, which can prevent the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin and lignin droplets during the bamboo pretreatment. The process parameters of DMC/OA pretreatment were optimized and discussed in terms of the removal of lignin and xylan, as well as enzymatic digestibility and bioethanol production. And complete characterizations (BET surface area, XRD, SEM, XPS, hydrophobicity, and FTIR technology) were further performed on the substrates to explain the mechanism of DMC-based DES pretreatment. And the native lignin in bamboo and regenerated DES lignin fraction were collected; the GPC and 2D-HSQC NMR techniques were used to characterize their chemical structure. Finally, the hydrogen bond number and interaction energy were measured to further explore the interaction mechanism between DMC-based DES system and bamboo biomass. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials *Dendrocalamus giganteus* Munro (*D. giganteus*, DG) harvested from Yunnan Province, China, was milled into bamboo powder (40–60 mesh) and dried in an oven at 40 °C for 10 h. Cellulase enzyme (CellicCTec2 with 220 FPU/mL and Celluclast 1.5 L with protein content of 40 mg/mL) was supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai). *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* from Yichang Angel Yeast Company was used during the ethanol fermentation. 2.2. DES pretreatment of bamboo residues The DMC (HBA) and oxalic acid (HBD) of different molar ratio were mixed at 90 °C until a homogeneous liquid formed. The Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters (α, β, and π*) were adopted to characterize these DES systems (Xue et al., 2016). Bamboo powder was pretreated with DMC-based DES at 110–140 °C and various times (3–8 h) with stirring of 150 rpm. The solid/liquid ratio of DG and DES was 1:10 (g/mL). After the pretreatment, the mixture was filtered using Brinell funnel, and the solid fractions were washed until neutral. The bamboo pretreated with DES was dried overnight in the oven of 40 °C for enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation. The liquid fraction was acidified to pH 2 with sulfuric acid to precipitate lignin. The lignin obtained was referred to as DMC/OA lignin. And the supernatant was collected for the DES recovery. The DES pretreated samples under the different conditions were named as DMC/OA-110 for the pretreatment temperature of 110 °C, DMC/OA-3 for pretreatment temperature of 3 h, and DMC/OA-1:1 for the DMC/OA ratio of 1:1, respectively. At the same time, bamboo powder pretreated with DES of ChCl/OA or liquid water hot under (LWH) a ratio of 1:10 (w/v) and 130 °C for 4 h was taken as control. The treated bamboo powder was labeled as ChCl/ OA-DG and LHW-DG, respectively. The NREL standard method was used to analyze the chemical composition of untreated and pretreated bamboo (Sluiter et al., 2011). The removal of xylan, delignification and glucan recovery after pretreatment were obtained by the formulas given below: Xylan removal (%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{xylan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{xylan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (1) Delignification(%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{lignin in treated bamboo(g)}}{\text{lignin in the raw biomass(g)}}$ × 100 (2) Glucan recovery(%) = $\frac{\text{glucan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{glucan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (3) 2.3. Enzymatic saccharification and fermentation of bamboo wastes Enzymatic hydrolysis of samples was operated in an air incubator (150 rpm and 50 °C) at 2 wt% solid concentration and 50 mM sodium citrate buffer solution for 72 h. The cellulase (Cellic® CTec2) was loaded at 20 FPU/g biomass. The hydrolysate was centrifuged and then analyzed the content of reducing sugars using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). On the other hand, Tween 80 of 150 mg/g substrates was added to further enhance the yield of glucose and xylose during the enzymatic hydrolysis. The enzymatic hydrolysate (16 mL) and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (3 g/L) were mixed at 35 °C for 24 h. The content of sugars and ethanol in the fermented broth were analyzed by HPLC (Agilent Technologies, 1260 series, USA), equipped with a Bio-Rad HPX-87 H column. The enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency and bioethanol production were calcu- lated, in accordance with our previous publications (Meng et al., 2023). 2.4. Cellulase adsorption study of treated biomass Enzymatic adsorption capacity was determined at 4 °C and 150 rpm by combining 10 mg of bamboo powder with the concentration range of (0.01–2) mg/mL cellulase solution (Yang et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023). The adsorption isotherms with different enzymatic concentrations were studied by UV-vis spectrophotometry after 3 h adsorption balance. The enzymatic adsorption capacity on solid residue were obtained by Langmuir isothermal adsorption equation (Γ = Гmax KC/(1+KC)), Γ and Γmax (mg/g) are the equilibrium and maximum adsorption capacity, respectively. C (mg/mg) the concentration of enzyme protein in the liquid. K (mL/mg cellulase) the constant of Langmuir. And the R (R=Γ max ×K) is the distribution coefficient (L/g). Effect of DMC/OA pretreatment on enzymatic adsorption and cellulose accessibility of bamboo biomass The effects of different pretreated samples on enzymatic adsorption are shown in Fig. 3. The ability of raw DG in adsorbing cellulase was weak and its maximum amount of adsorbed enzyme (Γmax), Langmuir constant (K) and distribution coefficient (R) were 13.83 mg/g sample, 4.96 mL/mg enzyme and 0.069 g/L, respectively. As shown in the adsorption isotherm, the enzyme adsorption capability on the substrates was promoted with the assistance of LHW and ChCL/OA pretreatment. Their maximum adsorption capacities were 7.08 and 18.03 mg/g sam-ple, increased by about 24% than that of untreated DG. The affinity of cellulase to substrate (the K value) also increased to 15.29 mL/mg for LHW-DG and 17.18 mL/mg for ChCL/OA-DG. Compared with LHW, ChCL/OA pretreatment showed the higher xylan removal yield. Theo-retically, the affinity of its substrate to cellulase should be stronger than LHW, because the xylan removal can result in the increase of substrates porosity. But there was no significant difference in the affinity of cellulase to the two pretreated substrates. This indicated that the surface and structural features of substrates might be the reasons for the inhibited cellulase adsorption on ChCL/OA-DG. However, when DG was performed the DMC/OA pretreatment, it was obvious that the cellulase showed higher affinity to the substrate based on adsorption curve and Langmuir constant (K), resulted in the higher adsorption capacity of cellulase on DMC/OA -DG (Γm=40.68 mg/g), meant that DMC/OA DES pretreatment created more binding sites of DG than the ChCL/OA pre-treatment. Probable reasons for this observation were that the removal of a large amount of lignin and hemicellulose, and the absence of surface covering on the pretreated substrate surface, which will be beneficial for enzyme adsorption and hydrolysis. The amount of cellulose surface area accessible to cellulase, defined as cellulose accessibility, also were used to predict the pretreatment performance of biomass. In Fig. 4b, the cellulose accessibility of untreated DG was only 55.46 mg dye/(g material), which is lower than that of untreated Moso bamboo (about 120 mg/g) reported by Ling et al. (2021). This was related to the content and structure of cellulose, xylan, and lignin in the raw bamboo. The value increased to 64.52 mg/g and 71.11 after LHW and ChCL/OA pretreatment, respectively. Compared with LHW-DG, the ChCL/OA-DG was not more susceptible to enzymatic saccharification despite having most of xylan removal, and its hydrolysis yield only increased to 13.44%. This observation indicates that some covering may be on the surface of ChCL/OA-DG, causing the decrease of cellulose accessibility and enzyme digestion efficiency. Mao et al. (2010) reported that the limitations of enzymatic hydrolysis for corn stover (CS) were caused by the limited accessibility of cellulose. The DMC/OA pretreat- ment resulted in 3.5-fold delignification than ChCL/OA pretreatment, so the cellulose accessibility of DMC/OA-DG was further improved to 95.15 mg/g, increased by 34% than that of ChCL/OA-DG, which is in accordance with the increase of enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency. Both ChCl and DMC are quaternary ammonium salts, but the alkyl chain length of DMC is longer than that of ChCl, which can affect the Kamlet-Taft parameters of DES system. As can be seen in Fig. 7a, the increase of α and π* value in ChCl/OA (1.802 and 1.408) was about 6% compared to these of DMC/OA. The α and π* values of two DES systems showed a slight difference due to the similar HBD. Liu et al. (2019) and Yu et al. This meant that DES of ChCl/OA should have better lignin solubility than DMC/OA. From the above discussion, multi-effects were revealed in the DMC/ OA pretreatment of bamboo residues. The DES system of DMC/OA with a long the alkyl chain length, had strong hydrogen bond acceptance ability and can destroy the hydrogen bond network structure of bamboo material. And the DMC/OA can not only catalyze the cleavage of the ether or ester bond between lignin and hemicellulose, but disrupted part of cellulose glycosidic bonds, ultimately leading to a decrease in cellu- lose polymerization and crystallinity degree. More importantly, the DMC/OA pretreatment has a significant self-cleaning effect on pseudo- lignin and surface lignin on the substrates. Additionally, due to the dissolution of lignin and xylan in the DMC-based DES system, the changes of hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity properties, crystal structures of cellulose, and cellulose accessibility were beneficial for the enzymatic saccharification. A new type of DMC/OA treated bamboo residue with self-cleaning function has been synthesized, which can clean the lignin droplets formed on the surface of substrate during the pretreatment process, and ultimately improve the enzymatic saccharification efficiency. ### 3.7. Mass balance analysis of ChCl/OA and DMC/OA pretreatment The pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation process of bamboo wastes are described in the mass balance image (Fig. 8). The 1000 g of DG including 474.7 g glucan, 166.1 g xylan and 283.1 g lignin were subjected to the DES pretreatment at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:10 at 130 °C for 4 h. When ChCl/OA was used as pretreatment solvent, 780.3 g of residue was recovered, which consisted of 402.1 g glucan, 1.2 g xylan and 213.7 g lignin. Then 54 g of glucose and a low ethanol content of 3.41 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 61.18%) was obtained during the enzymatic hydrolysis and fermenta- tion of ChCl/OA -DG. However, after DMC/OA pretreatment, 506.1 g pretreated DG were achieved, containing glucan of 411.9 g, xylan of 9.9 g and lignin of 52.4 g, indicating a large amount of lignin and hemicellulose have been removed, while most of the glucan was retained. Glucose of 224.2 g was released from the enzymatic hydrolysis process of DMC/OA-DG, with a glucose yield of 54.44%. The fermen- tation of hydrolysates resulted in the maximum ethanol production of 12.3 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 73.25%), which were 3.6- folds higher compared with that of ChCl/OA -DG. Previous studies based on various bamboo pretreatment were summarized (see supplementary material). It showed that the DMC-based DES pretreatment performance was at a moderate level among all bamboo pretreatments. The highest enzymatic hydrolysis yield (about 65%) comes from ternary DES pretreatment (ChCl/OA/EG), which is 1.18 times higher than DMC/OA pretreatment. During the pretreatment of ChCl/OA/EG, a third component, ethylene glycol, was required to alleviating the surface lignin and pseudo lignin on the substrates. DES of DMC/OA has similar to the effect of ternary DES pretreatment. Additionally, most methods improved the pretreatment performance of bamboo using the diverse hydrogen donors, while DMC, as hydrogen receptor, has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation, which DMC/OA pretreatment has potential in improving biorefinery efficiency of bamboo and reducing costs. ## 4. Conclusions A new green solvent DMC/OA with the self-cleaning lignin droplets function was used to treat bamboo at 130 °C and a solid-liquid ratio of 2:1 for 4 h. It removed a large amount of lignin and xylan from biomass, and the coverage of surface lignin was reduced to 56%, which increased the enzymatic digestibility by 4 times compared to ChCl-based DES. Higher cellulose accessibility, lower degree of polymerization, hydrophobicity and CrI/cellulose, and more porous structure of DMC/OA-DG were obtained. It provides some useful information for developing the functional DES pretreatment and more green solvents for the bamboo biorefinery. Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC) as a hydrogen bond acceptor, was used to synthesize a new deep eutectic solvent (DES) with self-cleaning lignin droplets function during the bamboo pretreatment. Introduction Bamboo, due to its fast growth rate (3–5 years) and chemical composition similar to wood, has become a promising biomass resource in biorefinery system (Scurlock, et al., 2000). Dendrocalamus giganteus Munro are planted widely in the southwest of China, and it was used as feedstock in the food, textile, construction, and papermaking industry. During these processes, approximately 3 million tons or more of bamboo processing residue are left annually (Liang et al., 2023). These bamboo wastes can be processed into sugar-based compounds and bioethanol through chemical or biochemical methods, which can reduce waste management and environmental pollution issues, and also provide sustainability for energy resources. Pretreatment technology was required to destroy the native recal- citrant structure of bamboo, making it easier for the carbohydrate fraction to hydrolyze into monosaccharides, and then ferment into ethanol (Ahmed et al., 2022; Anu et al., 2020). Deep eutectic solvent (DES) prepared with hydrogen bond donors (HBD) and acceptors (HBA) at proper ratios has attracted much interests of researcher due to ease of synthesis, less toxic, biodegradable, and low cost (Ahmed et al., 2022; Lugani et al., 2020). The biomass pretreatment of DES can efficiently remove non-crystalline complexes, such as hemicellulose and lignin, by breaking the lignin-carbohydrate linkages and ether bonds of lignin matrix (Jose et al., 2023; Areeya et al., 2023). Choline chloride (ChCl) was widely adopted as HBA in the synthesis of DES for biomass pre- treatment. A detailed discussion on ChCl-based DES pretreatment of lignocellulose have been proposed. Many studies have shown that the ChCl-based DES was a good solvent for lignin solubility and choline chloride increased the β-O-4 cleavage rate of milled wood lignin (Smink et al., 2019; Chen et al., 2020; Shen et al., 2020). Although the ChCl-based DES system has shown excellent perfor-mance in lignocellulose fractionation, other HBAs with special functions have also attracted the attention of some researchers, which had high biomass pretreatment performance and special functions in cracking the LCC linkages of biomass (Selkälä et al., 2016; Yang et al., 2022; Tang et al., 2023). Recently, Tang et al. (2023) reported a new type of DES with additional functions using CTAB and LA. They found that CTAB not only prevented the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin, but sol-ubilized some waxes on the substrates, significantly improving the accessibility of pretreated rice husks. Our previous results showed that DES pretreatment of tetramethylammonium chloride and oxalic acid can produce some lignin droplets on the pretreated substrates, which reduced the degradability of bamboo. These lignin droplets that affect carbohydrate bioconversion can be removed through washing the pre-treated residues with dilute alkaline solution (Yang et al., 2022). Methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (DMC), as an active monomer with unsaturated ethylene and quaternary ammonium salt groups, is widely used in the synthesis of various functional polymers, for example, polymerization of methacryloxyethyltrimethyl ammonium chloride (PDMC). The synthesis process of DMC has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation (Deng et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2016). Therefore, DMC, as a quaternary ammonium salt with longer alkyl chains, can also serve as a HBA in DES synthesis to form hydrogen bonds with hydrogen bond donors (HBD). The main objective of this study was to develop an innovative DMC-based DES pretreatment with self-cleaning functions, which can prevent the deposition and formation of pseudo lignin and lignin droplets during the bamboo pretreatment. The process parameters of DMC/OA pretreatment were optimized and discussed in terms of the removal of lignin and xylan, as well as enzymatic digestibility and bioethanol production. And complete characterizations (BET surface area, XRD, SEM, XPS, hydrophobicity, and FTIR technology) were further performed on the substrates to explain the mechanism of DMC-based DES pretreatment. And the native lignin in bamboo and regenerated DES lignin fraction were collected; the GPC and 2D-HSQC NMR techniques were used to characterize their chemical structure. Finally, the hydrogen bond number and interaction energy were measured to further explore the interaction mechanism between DMC-based DES system and bamboo biomass. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials *Dendrocalamus giganteus* Munro (*D. giganteus*, DG) harvested from Yunnan Province, China, was milled into bamboo powder (40–60 mesh) and dried in an oven at 40 °C for 10 h. Cellulase enzyme (CellicCTec2 with 220 FPU/mL and Celluclast 1.5 L with protein content of 40 mg/mL) was supplied by Sigma-Aldrich (Shanghai). *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* from Yichang Angel Yeast Company was used during the ethanol fermentation. 2.2. DES pretreatment of bamboo residues The DMC (HBA) and oxalic acid (HBD) of different molar ratio were mixed at 90 °C until a homogeneous liquid formed. The Kamlet-Taft empirical parameters (α, β, and π*) were adopted to characterize these DES systems (Xue et al., 2016). Bamboo powder was pretreated with DMC-based DES at 110–140 °C and various times (3–8 h) with stirring of 150 rpm. The solid/liquid ratio of DG and DES was 1:10 (g/mL). After the pretreatment, the mixture was filtered using Brinell funnel, and the solid fractions were washed until neutral. The bamboo pretreated with DES was dried overnight in the oven of 40 °C for enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation. The liquid fraction was acidified to pH 2 with sulfuric acid to precipitate lignin. The lignin obtained was referred to as DMC/OA lignin. And the supernatant was collected for the DES recovery. The DES pretreated samples under the different conditions were named as DMC/OA-110 for the pretreatment temperature of 110 °C, DMC/OA-3 for pretreatment temperature of 3 h, and DMC/OA-1:1 for the DMC/OA ratio of 1:1, respectively. At the same time, bamboo powder pretreated with DES of ChCl/OA or liquid water hot under (LWH) a ratio of 1:10 (w/v) and 130 °C for 4 h was taken as control. The treated bamboo powder was labeled as ChCl/ OA-DG and LHW-DG, respectively. The NREL standard method was used to analyze the chemical composition of untreated and pretreated bamboo (Sluiter et al., 2011). The removal of xylan, delignification and glucan recovery after pretreatment were obtained by the formulas given below: Xylan removal (%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{xylan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{xylan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (1) Delignification(%) = 1 - $\frac{\text{lignin in treated bamboo(g)}}{\text{lignin in the raw biomass(g)}}$ × 100 (2) Glucan recovery(%) = $\frac{\text{glucan in treated bamboo (g)}}{\text{glucan in the raw biomass (g)}}$ × 100 (3) 2.3. Enzymatic saccharification and fermentation of bamboo wastes Enzymatic hydrolysis of samples was operated in an air incubator (150 rpm and 50 °C) at 2 wt% solid concentration and 50 mM sodium citrate buffer solution for 72 h. The cellulase (Cellic® CTec2) was loaded at 20 FPU/g biomass. The hydrolysate was centrifuged and then analyzed the content of reducing sugars using high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC). On the other hand, Tween 80 of 150 mg/g substrates was added to further enhance the yield of glucose and xylose during the enzymatic hydrolysis. The enzymatic hydrolysate (16 mL) and *Saccharomyces cerevisiae* (3 g/L) were mixed at 35 °C for 24 h. The content of sugars and ethanol in the fermented broth were analyzed by HPLC (Agilent Technologies, 1260 series, USA), equipped with a Bio-Rad HPX-87 H column. The enzymatic hydrolysis efficiency and bioethanol production were calcu- lated, in accordance with our previous publications (Meng et al., 2023). 2.4. Compared with LHW, ChCL/OA pretreatment showed the higher xylan removal yield. Furthermore, the presence of lignin droplets on the surface of substrate also can lead to its high total lignin content during the ChCl/OA pre- treatment. From the above discussion, multi-effects were revealed in the DMC/ OA pretreatment of bamboo residues. The DES system of DMC/OA with a long the alkyl chain length, had strong hydrogen bond acceptance ability and can destroy the hydrogen bond network structure of bamboo material. And the DMC/OA can not only catalyze the cleavage of the ether or ester bond between lignin and hemicellulose, but disrupted part of cellulose glycosidic bonds, ultimately leading to a decrease in cellu- lose polymerization and crystallinity degree. More importantly, the DMC/OA pretreatment has a significant self-cleaning effect on pseudo- lignin and surface lignin on the substrates. Additionally, due to the dissolution of lignin and xylan in the DMC-based DES system, the changes of hydrophilicity/hydrophobicity properties, crystal structures of cellulose, and cellulose accessibility were beneficial for the enzymatic saccharification. A new type of DMC/OA treated bamboo residue with self-cleaning function has been synthesized, which can clean the lignin droplets formed on the surface of substrate during the pretreatment process, and ultimately improve the enzymatic saccharification efficiency. ### 3.7. Mass balance analysis of ChCl/OA and DMC/OA pretreatment The pretreatment, enzymatic hydrolysis and ethanol fermentation process of bamboo wastes are described in the mass balance image (Fig. 8). The 1000 g of DG including 474.7 g glucan, 166.1 g xylan and 283.1 g lignin were subjected to the DES pretreatment at a solid-liquid ratio of 1:10 at 130 °C for 4 h. When ChCl/OA was used as pretreatment solvent, 780.3 g of residue was recovered, which consisted of 402.1 g glucan, 1.2 g xylan and 213.7 g lignin. Then 54 g of glucose and a low ethanol content of 3.41 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 61.18%) was obtained during the enzymatic hydrolysis and fermenta- tion of ChCl/OA -DG. However, after DMC/OA pretreatment, 506.1 g pretreated DG were achieved, containing glucan of 411.9 g, xylan of 9.9 g and lignin of 52.4 g, indicating a large amount of lignin and hemicellulose have been removed, while most of the glucan was retained. Glucose of 224.2 g was released from the enzymatic hydrolysis process of DMC/OA-DG, with a glucose yield of 54.44%. The fermen- tation of hydrolysates resulted in the maximum ethanol production of 12.3 g/L (corresponding to ethanol yield of 73.25%), which were 3.6- folds higher compared with that of ChCl/OA -DG. Previous studies based on various bamboo pretreatment were summarized (see supplementary material). It showed that the DMC-based DES pretreatment performance was at a moderate level among all bamboo pretreatments. The highest enzymatic hydrolysis yield (about 65%) comes from ternary DES pretreatment (ChCl/OA/EG), which is 1.18 times higher than DMC/OA pretreatment. During the pretreatment of ChCl/OA/EG, a third component, ethylene glycol, was required to alleviating the surface lignin and pseudo lignin on the substrates. DES of DMC/OA has similar to the effect of ternary DES pretreatment. Additionally, most methods improved the pretreatment performance of bamboo using the diverse hydrogen donors, while DMC, as hydrogen receptor, has the advantages of low cost, low energy consumption, and ease of preparation, which DMC/OA pretreatment has potential in improving biorefinery efficiency of bamboo and reducing costs. ## 4. Conclusions A new green solvent DMC/OA with the self-cleaning lignin droplets function was used to treat bamboo at 130 °C and a solid-liquid ratio of 2:1 for 4 h. It removed a large amount of lignin and xylan from biomass, and the coverage of surface lignin was reduced to 56%, which increased the enzymatic digestibility by 4 times compared to ChCl-based DES. Higher cellulose accessibility, lower degree of polymerization, hydrophobicity and CrI/cellulose, and more porous structure of DMC/OA-DG were obtained. It provides some useful information for developing the functional DES pretreatment and more green solvents for the bamboo biorefinery.
